T3 Code

The open-source control plane for coding agents.

Download · iOS · Android · Web · Docs · Discord

T3 Code runs the coding agents on your machine and gives them one fast interface. Start a thread at your desk, then approve the next step from your phone. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity, Kiro, Pi, Muse Code, fx, and any [ACP](./docs/user/providers-acp.md) agent. If an agent is set up on your computer, T3 Code can control it. ## What you get - **Your subscriptions.** T3 Code does not resell tokens. It drives the agents you are already signed in to. - **Every agent in one place.** Change models in the middle of a thread. Let Claude hand a task to Codex. - **Desktop, web, and phone.** One server, and every client shows the same threads. There are apps for iOS and Android. - **Remote ready.** Run agents on any machine. Connect over your local network, Tailscale, or [T3 Connect](./docs/user/remote-access.md). - **Git built in.** Each thread can work in its own worktree. Review the diff, then commit, push, and open a pull request with one button. - **Fast.** Performance is a feature here. We measure it, and we treat a dropped frame as a bug. - **Open.** Source code is MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it under your own branding (see [Trademarks and forks](#trademarks-and-forks)). ## Install ### Desktop app [Download T3 Code](https://t3.codes/download) for macOS, Windows, or Linux. You can also use a package manager: | Platform | Command | | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | macOS | `brew install --cask t3-code` | | Windows | `winget install T3Tools.T3Code` or `scoop install extras/t3code` | | Arch Linux | `yay -S t3code-bin` | | Nix | `nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code` | | Debian, Ubuntu | `.deb` from [Releases](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases) | ### Command line This installs the `t3` command. Run `t3` to start the server and open the web app. ```bash curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex ``` To try it once without an install, run `npx t3@latest`. ### Phone Get the app from the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/t3-code-remote-claude-more/id6787819824) or [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.t3tools.t3code). Then follow [remote access](./docs/user/remote-access.md) to connect it to your computer. ### Sign in to an agent T3 Code needs one agent that is installed and signed in. For example, install [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) and run `claude auth login`, or install [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) and run `codex login`. [Provider setup](./docs/user/install.md#providers) has the steps for each agent. [Install T3 Code](./docs/user/install.md) covers nightly builds, AppImage, WSL, and NixOS. ## "Wait, what are you selling me?" Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar. We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork the source code and build the tool that you want, under your own name and branding. ## Documentation - [Install and first run](./docs/user/install.md) - [Remote access from a phone or another machine](./docs/user/remote-access.md) - [Permission modes](./docs/user/permission-modes.md) - [Source control](./docs/user/source-control.md) - [Connect outside agents over MCP](./docs/user/outside-agents.md) - [FAQ](./docs/user/faq.md) [All docs](./docs/README.md) has the full list. ## Contributing We have limited review capacity. Small, focused fixes are the most likely to be merged. Features need an approved discussion first. - Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) before you report a bug or open a pull request. - Put feature requests in [Ideas](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/discussions/categories/ideas). - Build from source with the [development runbook](./docs/operations/00_development.md#first-checkout). The [architecture overview](./docs/internals/01_architecture.md) explains how it works. - Get help in [Discord](https://discord.gg/jn4EGJjrvv). ## License The source code in this repository is licensed under the [MIT License](./LICENSE). ## Trademarks and forks The MIT license applies **only to the source code**. It does not grant any rights to T3 Tools, Inc.'s trademarks, branding, or trade dress, including the **T3 Code** name, wordmark, logos, and application icons. If you fork, redistribute, or build on T3 Code's source code: - **Use your own branding.** Replace the T3 Code name, wordmark, logos, and application icons in any public fork, redistributed build, website, package, or app store listing. - **Be explicitly clear that your project is unofficial.** Do not use the T3 Code name, wordmark, logo, or branding in your own projects without making it unmistakably clear that your project is unofficial and not affiliated with or endorsed by T3 Tools, Inc. Using our name, wordmark, logo, or branding in a way that suggests official status or affiliation is trademark infringement and unlawful. **Any project indicating or implying that it is an official version of T3 Code when it is not will be pursued to the full extent of the law.** See [TRADEMARK.md](./TRADEMARK.md) for the full trademark and branding policy.

Orca

中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Español · Français · Português · Türkçe · Русский

Bots inside your agent IDE.

Open source. Bring your own everything: your Claude Code or Codex, your local or remote machines, your tools. Ask from Slack or your phone. When it needs you, it's one tab away.

Download Orca  ·  Explore bots →

## Features
### Orca Bots Ask a bot in Slack, Linear, or GitHub to fix a bug, and come back to a tested pull request. It runs on your own Claude Code or Codex. Open its work in Orca to review it or step in. [Overview](https://orca.dev/bots) · [Security](https://orca.dev/docs/bots/security) · [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/bots)
### Chat or Terminal Run any agent in Chat UI or as the raw CLI, and move a conversation between the two without losing context. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/agents/native-chat)
### Orchestrate Agents Hand a big task to one agent. It splits the work, starts worker agents in their own workspaces, and brings their results back to you. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/orchestration)
### Run Anywhere Pair a Remote Orca Server, work on any SSH host, or give a worktree its own cloud VM. Your agents keep running when your laptop sleeps. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/ways-to-run)
### Mobile App Pair Orca with the mobile app to get pinged when an agent needs you, reply in chat, and keep work moving on any of your machines when you are away from your desk. [iOS App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/orca-ide/id6766130217) · [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=dev.orca.app) · [Android APK](https://orca.dev/download/android) · [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/mobile)
### Review AI Output Review diffs, leave notes on exact changed lines, and send focused feedback back to an agent. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/review/annotate-ai-diff)
### Git Integration Draft commit messages and pull requests from the diff, then send failing checks or PR review comments back to an agent to fix. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/review/commit-push)
### Parallel Worktrees Quickly split tasks into isolated environments, so multiple agents can work side by side without interfering with each other. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/model/worktrees)
### Design Mode Click any element in Orca's browser to copy its HTML, styles, and selector, then paste it into your agent's chat. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/browser/design-mode)
### GitHub & Linear, Native See your GitHub and Linear tasks in one place, and start a workspace for each when you're ready to build. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/review/linear)
### Orca CLI Anything you can do in Orca, your agents can do too: create worktrees, start workers, drive the browser and desktop apps, and schedule automations, all from the command line. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/overview)
### Plugins Themes, editors, languages, and panels from the community, installed in a click. [Browse plugins →](https://orca.dev/plugins)
### Split Anything Put agents, terminals, browsers, and diffs side by side in split panes shaped to the task. [Docs →](https://orca.dev/docs/model/tabs-panes-splits)
**Also in the box:** - **[Bot Schedules & Triggers](https://orca.dev/docs/bots#put-it-on-a-schedule)**: run a bot every weekday at 9, or when a pull request opens, a check fails, or a webhook fires. - **[Bot Memory in Markdown](https://orca.dev/docs/bots/security#what-you-can-review)**: a bot's soul and memory are plain Markdown files (`SOUL.md`, `MEMORY.md`) you can read and edit. - **[Drag Files to Agents](https://orca.dev/docs/editing/file-explorer)**: drag files from the explorer, or images from your desktop, straight into an agent's prompt. - **[Jump Anywhere](https://orca.dev/docs/model/quick-open)**: one shortcut jumps to any workspace or tab across every repo and host. - **[Rich Previews](https://orca.dev/docs/editing/viewers)**: open images, PDFs, and Markdown right in the workspace, next to the agent that made them. - **[Mobile Emulator](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/overview#mobile-emulator)**: run an iOS Simulator or Android emulator beside your agent, and let it tap, type, and check its own work. - **[Dictation](https://orca.dev/docs/settings#voice)**: press a shortcut and talk. Orca types what you say into the agent's prompt or terminal. - **[Usage & Accounts](https://orca.dev/docs/agents/usage-tracking)**: see how much of your agent limits you've used and when they reset, and switch accounts without logging out. - **[Automations](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/automations)**: schedule prompts to run on any repo: nightly dependency bumps, weekly triage, flaky-test sweeps. - **[Computer Use](https://orca.dev/docs/cli/computer-use)**: when there's no CLI or API, agents can see and drive desktop apps and external browsers. - **And many, many more**: we ship daily, so this list is perpetually behind. The [changelog](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases) is the real feature list. --- ## Supported Agents Works with **any CLI agent** — if it runs in a terminal, it runs in Orca.

Claude Code   Codex   Grok   Cursor   GitHub Copilot   Muse   DeepSeek Harness   ZCode   OpenCode   MiMo Code   Amp   OpenClaude   Antigravity   Pi   oh-my-pi   Hermes Agent   Devin   Goose   Auggie   Autohand Code   Charm   Cline   CodeBuddy   Codebuff   Freebuff   Command Code   Continue   Droid   Kilocode   Kimi   Kiro   Mistral Vibe   Qwen Code   Rovo Dev   + any CLI agent

--- ## Install ### Desktop — macOS, Windows, Linux - **[Download from orca.dev](https://orca.dev/download)** - Or grab a build directly: [macOS Apple Silicon](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/orca-macos-arm64.dmg) · [macOS Intel](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/orca-macos-x64.dmg) · [Windows (.exe)](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/orca-windows-setup.exe) · [Linux AppImage](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/orca-linux.AppImage) · [All builds](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest) _Or via a package manager:_ ```bash # macOS (Homebrew) # Always use the full name; bare `orca` is an unrelated Plotly cask. brew install --cask stablyai/orca/orca # Upgrade an existing install brew upgrade --cask stablyai/orca/orca # Release candidates (conflicts with the stable cask; uninstall it first) brew install --cask stablyai/orca/orca@rc # Arch Linux (AUR) — or stably-orca-git to build from source yay -S stably-orca-bin ``` ### Mobile App — iOS, Android Pair with your desktop app to monitor and steer your agents from your phone. - **iOS:** [Download on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/orca-ide/id6766130217) - **Android:** [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=dev.orca.app) · [Download APK](https://orca.dev/download/android) · [Install guide](https://orca.dev/docs/android-apk) --- ## Community & Support - **Discord:** Join the community on **[Discord](https://discord.gg/fzjDKHxv8Q)**. - **Twitter / X:** Follow **[@orca_build](https://x.com/orca_build)** for updates and announcements. - **WeChat:** Scan to join an Orca community WeChat group. - **Feedback & Ideas:** We ship fast. Missing something? [Request a new feature](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues). - **Privacy:** See the [privacy & telemetry docs](https://orca.dev/docs/telemetry) for what anonymous usage data Orca collects and how to opt out. - **Show Support:** [Star](https://github.com/stablyai/orca) this repo to follow along with our daily ships. --- ## Developing Want to contribute or run locally? See our [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) guide.

## Signed Builds Windows code signing sponsored/provided by [SignPath.io](https://signpath.io), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org). ## License Orca is free and open source under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

items.description: Does GTA VI run on PC yet? A live tracker of community recompilation and emulation efforts, updated daily.
items.readme_text:
# PortWatch VI

**Does GTA VI run on PC yet?** A static GitHub Pages site that tracks every serious community effort to recompile, emulate or port the leaked Xbox Series build of GTA VI to PC. All efforts are scored on one ladder, and a scout refreshes the data every 3 hours.

- One headline progress bar shows the closest effort, with the top projects pinned to it.
- A live countdown runs to the missing executable's expected drop.
- A leaderboard card per effort shows its own bar, milestone ladder, groundwork breakdown, what works and what's blocking.
- Further sections cover the watchlist of early projects, a toolkit of asset tools, the scout's inbox of new candidates, and fake-download warnings.

No game files, keys or executables are hosted or linked, ever.

## Deploy on GitHub Pages

1. Create a new GitHub repository and push this folder to its `main` branch.
2. In the repo, open **Settings → Pages** and set **Source** to **GitHub Actions**.
3. Open **Settings → Actions → General** and make sure workflows are allowed.
4. Open **Actions → Scout → Run workflow** to run the first scout. It commits fresh data and deploys the site.

Each deploy also runs `scripts/build-site.mjs`, which turns `data/tracker.json` into pages search engines can read: one page per news story (`news/<id>.html`), a news archive, an RSS feed (`news/feed.xml`) and `sitemap.xml`. It then pings [IndexNow](https://www.indexnow.org/) (Bing, Yandex and others; no account needed) with the URLs that changed since the last deploy. For Google, add the site in Search Console and submit `sitemap.xml`.

From then on, `Scout` runs every 3 hours (00:17, 03:17, 06:17 … UTC) on GitHub's servers, so no computer of yours needs to be on. Any push to `main` redeploys the site through `Deploy site`. To change the frequency, edit the `cron` line in `.github/workflows/scout.yml`. For example, `17 6 * * *` runs it once a day. GitHub can delay scheduled runs by a few minutes when it's busy.

## What the scout does (`scripts/scout.mjs`)

1. **Refreshes** every tracked repo: stars, forks, issues, last push, commits in the last 7 days, and whether it's gone (404, or 451 for a DMCA block). It also hashes each README to notice changes.
2. **Spots claims.** If a README newly says GTA VI boots, reaches the menu or runs at some FPS, the card shows an "unverified claim" banner and the change feed records it.
3. **Discovers** new repos from GitHub and GitLab searches (`scout.queries` in `data/tracker.json`), Hacker News, Bluesky, Mastodon, Lemmy and 4chan, plus Reddit and X when keys are set, by pulling GitHub links out of posts. It also gathers **headlines** from the Google News and Bing News feeds, keeping only stories about the leak, ports, takedowns, scams or official news. And it **watches GitHub's public DMCA log** for new Take-Two or Rockstar notices, flagging any tracked project they name. On 4chan it uses the free read-only API, at one request per second. It opens only /v/ threads that mention GTA VI together with port terms (recomp, emulator, leak, executable, GitHub…), plus /vg/'s /gtag/ and /emugen/ generals. Change the boards with `scout.chan.boards`. Nothing from 4chan is shown on the site except, indirectly, repo names that pass every filter.
4. **Filters out spam** such as clone networks, download lures and "PC installer" repos. Their names are counted under *There is no download*, never linked.
5. **Filters out copies.** Re-uploads of tracked projects are flagged when they reuse a tracked project's name or have a README that is 60% or more identical, renamed copies included. Original fan games and repos without a real README are skipped too. Candidates already waiting are re-checked every run.
6. **Scores substance** from code language, size, technical depth, status tables, tests and commit activity. Repos with real code go to **New candidates**, shown as plain text and not linked until reviewed. Thin or off-topic ones are remembered and skipped.
7. **Writes news** (needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). Claude searches the web for takedowns, bans, confirmed leaks, legal news, scams and official announcements, then writes up to two short original articles. It runs at most every 11 hours, not on every 3-hourly scout run, to keep costs down. A source is kept only if it came up in Claude's own search. Each article's image is the source's preview image, credited and linked back; it falls back to a generated cover.
8. **Records** a change feed, the day's leader score for the sparkline, and a run summary.

### Optional secrets (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions)

| Secret | What it enables |
|---|---|
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | **Claude review.** When a tracked README changes, or a new candidate shows up, Claude (`claude-opus-5-5`) reads the README and recent commits and re-scores the effort. It also promotes or rejects candidates automatically. Guardrails clamp the output: a GTA VI milestone only counts if Claude quotes text that really appears in the repo, and groundwork can rise at most 0.3 per run. Reviews are capped at 12 per run. Each costs very roughly $0.05–0.20, depending on README size. |
| `REDDIT_CLIENT_ID` / `REDDIT_CLIENT_SECRET` | Reddit search. Reddit blocks anonymous API and RSS access, so Reddit is skipped without these. The API is free for small non-commercial use, but since late 2025 every new app needs Reddit's manual approval. Create a "script" app at reddit.com/prefs/apps, request access, and paste the client ID and secret here once approved. |
| `X_BEARER_TOKEN` | X recent search. This needs a paid X API tier. |

Without any secrets the scout still runs on every keyless source, and new finds wait in *New candidates* for review.

### Daily Claude editor (alternative to an API key)

Instead of `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, a scheduled Claude session on the maintainer's PC can run once a day, following [EDITOR.md](EDITOR.md). It re-scores changed projects, reviews candidates, verifies leads, keeps the countdown accurate and writes news, then commits `data/tracker.json`. It also reads 4chan's /v/, /vg/ and /g/ in full through `tools/chan-scan.ps1`, which gathers GTA VI port discussion from live threads and the public archives into a local digest (`.chan/`, never committed). The scout only picks GitHub links out of those threads. It uses the maintainer's Claude plan and needs no separate billing. It runs while the Claude desktop app is open; a missed run happens on the next launch.

## Editing the data by hand

Everything lives in `data/tracker.json`:

- `efforts[]`: each effort has a `tier` (`tracked` puts it in the race, `watchlist` lists it below). Each also carries `groundwork` (four 0–1 values), `gta` (`loads`/`boots`/`menu`/`ingame` are 0, 0.5 or 1, plus `fps` and `stability`), and short `highlights` and `blockers`.
- `exe`: drives the countdown. If the release time is announced, set `expectedAt` (ISO time) and `timeAnnounced: true`. When it drops, set `status: "released"` and `releasedAt`, and the countdown turns into a "time since release" clock.
- `candidates[]`: move one into `efforts` to promote it, or into `ignored` to dismiss it.
- `site.heroImage`: the hero photo (see below). An optional `site.heroCredit` adds a credit line under it.

Scoring is in `assets/js/scoring.js`, shared by the site and the scout. Groundwork fills 0–25%. After that, milestones sit at Exe runs 25, First frame 40, Main menu 55, In-game 70, 30 FPS 85 and Stable 100.

## Hero photo

The hero shows an original sunset illustration until the photo loads. The photo is `assets/img/hero-miami.jpg` (2400px wide): Brickell, Miami, at night, by Steele Rutherford on Unsplash, free to use under the Unsplash License without a credit line. `assets/img/social-miami.jpg` (1200×630) is the share card, made from the same photo. Give a replaced image a new filename: images are cached for 4 hours in browsers and for days by link previews. Don't use GTA VI artwork or footage there.

## Local preview

Any static server works. On Windows without Node or Python:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools/serve.ps1 -Port 8080
```

Then open http://localhost:8080. To try the scout locally with Node 20+, run `node scripts/scout.mjs --dry-run`. Setting `GITHUB_TOKEN` avoids the 60-requests-per-hour anonymous limit.

## Disclaimer

Fan-made and unofficial. Not affiliated with Rockstar Games, Take-Two or Microsoft. Scores are editorial estimates from public READMEs, commits and issues, and self-reported claims are labelled. Maintainers who think their project is mis-scored can open an issue with evidence.

# dsh-our-free-model **简体中文** | [English](README_EN.md)

Trendshift JavaScript 周榜第 1 · 2026-10-05 至 2026-10-11 · 更新中，截至 2026-10-11
> 在 dsh 里装上插件即可使用免费车道，无需登录、注册或填写 API Key。 > > *Install the plugin in dsh to use the free lane without signing in, creating an > account, or entering an API key.* > > 模型清单跟随上游刷新，可用性由**你自己这台机器的网络出口**实测得出， > 思考强度下发的是真实预算而不是提示词，另附一个 OpenAI 兼容的本地转发端口。 > > 纯插件挂载：不改内核、无构建步骤、零依赖。
--- ## 交流群

QQ 群：974582805（OFM技术交流[2群]）
扫码加入群聊，一起交流插件使用心得、反馈问题与分享玩法。
--- ## 亮点 - **开箱即用，无配置环节**——不需要账号、不需要 Key、不需要在后台申请配额。 - **上游来源公开透明**——免费车道来源为 [OpenCode 的 Zen 网关](https://opencode.ai)，Kilo 渠道来源为 [Kilo AI 的公共网关](https://kilo.ai)，均直连、不经任何第三方中转。请求由谁处理、数据发往何处，见「上游是哪些源」与「免责声明」。 - **清单跟随上游**——模型集合、上下文长度与能力在每次刷新时向上游重新拉取，插件内不保存静态快照。 - **选择器只广播可用的模型**——上游清单已声明但网关明确拒绝路由的模型（返回 `Model is unavailable`、或 404 找不到该 id）从下拉框移除，仅在设置页保留记录并注明拒因；网关自身故障（5xx）、配额限制（429）、超时与断网不属于对模型的判定，一律保持可达；被地区策略拦截的模型归入 region-limited 分组。整轮探测全部被拒时同样保留，选择器不会为空。 - **公告中心 + 实时推送**——仓库维护者在仓库中编辑 JSON 并推送后，所有已安装实例最迟在一个轮询周期内收到；正文为白名单约束下的 HTML，支持图文排版；`urgent` 级别触发全屏弹窗；可选系统级通知。 - **应用内升级**——设置页一键升级：下载 → SHA-256 校验 → 备份 → 原子替换 → 校验回读 → 热重载，任一步失败自动回滚至上一版本。 - **热重载**——升级与代码变更即时生效，无需重启应用；也可在设置页手动触发，或启用文件监视自动重载。 - **按响应体形状判定流式响应**——网关在高负载下会以 BUSL-1.1）：工具输出过滤器的最早参考。`src/token-saver/compact/` 已全部重写，仅保留 RTK 的输出标记与阈值——那些标记是模型读惯的线格式，改掉会改变模型行为而不是让代码更原创。2.8.6 的替换范围见 [验证记录](docs/verification/2026-11-18-independent-core.md)。 根目录的 MIT 只覆盖 OFM 自己写的代码；上面仍在使用的组件和数据按各自许可证提供，完整条款以上游 LICENSE 为准。这份名单是来源记录，不改变任何组件的许可证。 ## Star 趋势 图表由 Star History 自动更新，无需手动提交图片。受服务缓存（当前为 24 小时）和 GitHub 图片缓存影响，显示可能延迟，并非秒级实时；点击图表可查看在线趋势。

# ARTEX **Autonomous penetration testing that keeps its receipts.** Self-hosted multi-agent offensive security. A planner explores, workers run real tools, and every finding stays bound to the assets and HTTP traffic that prove it. [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/BaaRai/ARTEX?label=release&color=6b34db)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](LICENSE) [![CI](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Go](https://img.shields.io/github/go-mod/go-version/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](go.mod) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-join%20the%20server-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/VKyvMTcgXh) [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Screenshots](#screenshots) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#installation) · [Configuration](#configuration) · [Security](SECURITY.md) [![Join us on Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/JOIN%20US%20ON-DISCORD-5865F2?style=for-the-badge&logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/VKyvMTcgXh)
--- ARTEX is a self-hosted, LLM-driven penetration testing platform. It is not a chat wrapper around a scanner: a planner splits a goal into intents, workers execute them with real tools, and the results are written back into **two linked graphs**: one for what you know about the target, one for how the test is progressing. Every finding can carry the captured request and response that justify it, and every autonomous action passes through scope rules, approval gates and budgets. - **It explores, it doesn't chat.** Goal decomposition, intent dispatch, worker execution and write-back form a closed loop that keeps advancing until the goal is proven. - **Two graphs, one audit trail.** The shared asset graph says *what exists*; the per-task exploration graph says *what was tried, what it produced, and why*. Anchors link the two. - **Findings with evidence.** A recording MITM proxy and a browser extension capture real traffic; findings, evidence quotes and retests are tied to the exact request/response. - **Autonomy with brakes.** Human-in-the-loop approvals, argv-prefix rules, scope/deny gates, token and turn budgets, a target noise governor, and prompt-injection framing on tool output. - **Self-hosted and model-agnostic.** One Go binary with the Next.js UI embedded, PostgreSQL, your own Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a local Ollama. --- ## Quick start ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD (and optionally an LLM key) docker compose up -d --build # builds from this checkout, starts PostgreSQL ``` Open **http://localhost:8787**. On the first visit `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup: ```bash docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token" ``` > Multi-arch release images (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) are published to GitHub Container > Registry at `ghcr.io/baarai/artex` from the next tagged release; v0.7.0 predates the publish > step. For pulling the prebuilt image and all other installation paths (script, binaries, > source, release archives), see [Installation](#installation). --- ## Multi-provider workers In **System → LLM**, configure the profiles you want to use. In **System → Settings**, set the concurrent worker count to at least **2** before starting a task (the count applies to subsequently started tasks). In **System → Agents → Worker**, leave the model set to follow the task; a fixed Worker model takes precedence over rotation. When creating a task, select both profiles in **LLM config chain**, arrange their order, and enable **Enable multi-LLM worker rotation**. For an existing task, open its LLM config control, change the switch or profile order, and save. Rotation assigns successive worker intents A, B, A, B, regardless of completion order. Separate intents can run concurrently on different providers; each intent keeps its selected provider unless it fails over. Planner and other unbound roles continue using the task's current profile. Turning rotation off restores ordered task-level failover. An excluded provider is skipped, so an intent pinned to an exhausted profile falls back to the task's current profile instead of retrying it; rotation keeps cycling the whole list and does not rebalance around a dead provider. Saving the chain resets their failure state. Changes do not interrupt in-flight calls. The rotation cursor starts again after a server restart and saving the chain does not reset it; the profile order and switch remain persisted. The task creation and `PUT /api/tasks/{id}/llm` APIs accept `llm_rotate: true` alongside the ordered `llm_profile_ids`. Omitting `llm_rotate` on an update preserves its value. ## Screenshots | Tasks | Findings | | :---: | :---: | | ![Tasks](screenshots/tasks.png) | ![Findings](screenshots/findings.png) | | Task execution: sessions and tool calls | Exploration graph | | :---: | :---: | | ![Execution](screenshots/sessions.png) | ![Exploration graph](screenshots/graph.png) | | Asset coverage graph | Traffic recording | | :---: | :---: | | ![Asset coverage graph](screenshots/assets_test.png) | ![Traffic](screenshots/traffic.png) | | Human-in-the-loop chat | Interception approvals | | :---: | :---: | | ![Chat](screenshots/chat.png) | ![Interception](screenshots/intercept.png) |
More screenshots (assets, agents, LLM, logs) | Assets | Agent management | | :---: | :---: | | ![Assets](screenshots/assets.png) | ![Agent](screenshots/agents.png) | | LLM configuration | Backend logs | | :---: | :---: | | ![LLM](screenshots/llm.png) | ![Logs](screenshots/logs.png) |
--- ## How it works ### Dual-graph architecture: exploration graph + asset graph ARTEX separates *what the goals are* from *how far testing has progressed* into two independent graphs linked by anchors: - **Asset graph (shared across tasks).** One source of truth for `root_domain / subdomain / ip / service / app / endpoint`, owned by companies. Parent-child relationships and deduplication keys are computed by the program; agents only submit raw observations. - **Exploration graph (per task).** The task's reasoning and progress: `goal / intent / fact / finding / hint` nodes connected by `spawns / derived_from / yields / proves` edges into a lineage chain. - **Anchors link them.** `exploration_anchors(node_id, asset_id)` ties intents, facts and findings to concrete assets: which assets a direction touched, and which intents tested a given asset. This also powers **asset test coverage** and the coverage graph. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph EG["Exploration graph (per-task · advance chain)"] direction TB G["goal"] I1["intent A"] F1["fact"] I2["intent B"] FD["finding (vulnerability)"] G -->|spawns| I1 I1 -->|yields| F1 F1 -->|derived_from| I2 I2 -->|proves| FD end subgraph AG["Asset graph (globally shared · source of truth)"] direction TB RD["root_domain"] SD["subdomain"] SV["service"] EP["endpoint"] RD --> SD --> SV --> EP end I1 -. anchor .-> SD F1 -. anchor .-> SV I2 -. anchor .-> EP FD -. anchor .-> EP ``` The **planner** reads the exploration graph, judges goals, and dispatches intents only when there is an uncovered direction; a **worker** claims one intent, executes it, writes assets/facts/findings back into both graphs, then stops. ### The engine loop The engine is event-driven: any graph change wakes the planner, workers claim and execute intents, write-back triggers the next round, until `prove_goal` closes the task. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant EV as graph-change debounce participant P as planner participant FR as frontier intent queue participant W as worker participant PX as recording proxy participant DB as dual graphs + activity EV-->>P: wake up P->>DB: read situation (graph_overview prefetch + coverage/scope) P->>FR: dispatch 0..N intents (with asset_ids) Note over P,FR: most wake-ups dispatch 0 (no new direction means done) W->>FR: claimNext claims one intent W->>DB: fetch the raw assets of the intent's asset_ids W->>PX: real tool execution (Kali / Bash / HTTP) PX-->>W: response (fully traced + CA verified) W->>DB: write back fact / asset / finding + per-step activity DB-->>EV: graph change EV-->>P: wake again (closed loop) ``` ### Durable attack chains, shared worker memory Real attack chains are multi-step and ordered (find an injection → get credentials → move laterally). The planner keeps a **todolist retained per task across wake-ups**: it records the chain once, then dispatches the next step only when its prerequisites are satisfied by facts. Workers can also **search each other's execution traces** (`search_all_worker_traces`, `list_worker_traces`, `get_worker_trace`). Observations that never became formal facts (an error message, a response snippet, a hidden parameter) are still reusable by the next worker, while each worker remains confined to the intent it claimed. --- ## Features ### Evidence, not chat logs - **Recording MITM proxy** (`:8788`) with a generated CA: every Bash/HTTP tool call is traced, and request/response evidence can be bound to a finding. - **Browser extension** (`extension/`) for authenticated targets: log in once (captcha, email OTP, 2FA included), capture the session, and the requests/responses land in the same traffic store.
Using the traffic capture extension - Load the unpacked extension from `extension/` (Chrome/Edge: Developer Mode → Load unpacked); - In the popup, set your ARTEX URL and token, then press **Start capture** on the tab you are browsing; - Use the site normally; text requests/responses are batched to `POST /api/traffic/ingest` (authenticated). Binary bodies (images, fonts) are skipped, bodies are truncated at 256 KiB, batches are capped at 50 entries; - Press **Stop** when done. Everything stays in your local traffic store.
- **Verified findings**: findings carry a POE level, a verification status and a note; a finding is `verified` only when a bound proof/response and verbatim evidence quotes support it. Gzip/deflate bodies are decoded before the quote check. The findings table supports bulk status updates, and the report and export show each finding's proof strength next to its status. - **Traffic replay**: open a captured exchange and replay the recorded request (method, URL, headers and stored body) from the traffic detail; replay stays disabled while only the body preview is loaded. - **Vulnerability retest loop**: a dedicated `retester` agent re-runs a finding with optional fixed version/conditions, records `Still reproducible / Fixed / Cannot confirm`, and can move the finding to `Fixed` automatically. Original evidence and reports are preserved. - **Reports and exports**: findings, evidence and task archives, with traffic snapshots kept encrypted at rest. ### Control without slowing down - **Interception gate**: every tool call can require human approval, with rules by `string`, `regex` or **argv prefix**. An argv rule is a JSON array of 1 to 8 tokens (Bash only, for example `["git","push"]`); it matches only a single simple command whose parsed prefix equals the pattern exactly. Pipes, lists, redirections, prefix assignments, subshells, background jobs, wrapper programs and command/parameter substitutions do not match; flags are ignored by construction (`["git","push"]` covers `git push --force`, but `git -C /repo push` matches nothing). Each approval records who decided: `human`, `rule`, `model` or `system`. - **Scope and target gate**: scope rows define the coverage denominator; assets outside the declared scope are not explored. The target gate (off by default, API-only) can refuse destinations that were not approved. - **Budgets**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a whole task (planner and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Near the limit the task enters a forced wrap-up; a worker is not started when the remaining budget cannot cover it. Spend already in `llm_usage` is restored after a restart. A task that is already inside the wrap-up reserve only has that reserve left, so the revived run wraps up instead of starting another worker. The per-worker cost estimate starts again from the defaults (50,000 tokens and 10 turns) until a worker finishes in this process. - **Noise governor**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE=quiet|balanced|aggressive` paces requests ARTEX sends to targets (per-host rate, burst, in-flight limit, jitter, backoff on 429/503, short GET caching). With a profile set, agents also receive low-and-slow flags for the installed scanners. - **Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Disable with `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0`. ### Assets and coverage - **Coverage ledger and force-directed coverage graph**: in-scope assets are highlighted as tested or untested, with linked intents, facts and findings per node. - **Company-scoped asset graph**: shared across tasks, deduplicated by the program, with domain → subdomain → service → endpoint containment. - **ScopeSentry sync**: pull asset data from a [ScopeSentry](https://github.com/Autumn-27/ScopeSentry) instance by project or task, merged by company scope into the asset graph for agents to explore.
Syncing from ScopeSentry - On the **Asset Sync** page, enter the ScopeSentry address and API key; - Choose the targets and asset types by **project** or **task** (domains / subdomains / IPs / ports / sites / endpoints…); - Import: rows are merged by company asset scope and become part of the asset graph.
- **Task categories, templates, relations and archives** for repeatable engagements. ### Platform - **LLM profiles with failover**: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible relays and keyless Ollama; multiple profiles per task with automatic failover. - **Token accounting**: per-task and per-session usage, cache reads/writes, and an LLM record view for every call. - **MCP servers, skills, memory and a workspace**: extend the agent with remote tools and reusable prompt/playbook material. - **Web search**: the agent's search tool uses Brave, Tavily or the opt-in Keenable backend, configured in **System → Settings** with the key encrypted at rest; search can also egress through its own proxy. - **Single binary**: the Next.js UI is embedded with `go:embed`; PostgreSQL is the only external dependency. --- ## Installation > Requires **PostgreSQL**; exploration requires an **LLM** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or > `OPENAI_API_KEY`, also configurable in the UI). ### Option 1: one-click install script (recommended) ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX ./install.sh ``` The script detects or installs Docker, then offers **① all-Docker** (writes `.env`, runs `docker compose up -d --build`) or **② local build and run** (generates `config.json`, builds the embedded binary, starts it). Open **http://localhost:8787**; `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup (`docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token"`). The UI listens on `127.0.0.1` by default. To reach it from another machine (or from Windows when ARTEX runs inside WSL), set `ARTEX_BIND_ADDR=0.0.0.0` in `.env` (the setup token still protects the first-run claim), or keep loopback and use a reverse proxy or SSH tunnel. ### Option 2: Docker (Compose checkout build or prebuilt GHCR image) Build from a checkout with Docker Compose: ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD, optionally ANTHROPIC_API_KEY docker compose up -d --build # → http://localhost:8787 ``` The checkout build needs the Docker **buildx** plugin (BuildKit). Docker Desktop and get.docker.com include it; distro packages and Homebrew's docker CLI (Colima) may not. If `docker buildx version` fails, install `docker-buildx-plugin` or `docker-buildx`, or on macOS `brew install docker-buildx`. Without it the build stops at the first stage with `failed to parse platform`. The release workflow publishes a multi-arch image (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) to GitHub Container Registry on each `v*` tag, with tags `:latest`, `:v`, and `:`. v0.7.0 predates that step, so there is no `artex` package yet: until the next tagged release, use the checkout build above, and `docker-compose.ghcr.yml` and the `docker pull` below will fail with `denied`. GHCR packages start private; after the first publish the package visibility must be set to Public, and the release workflow verifies that the image pulls anonymously and fails the job otherwise. Once the image is published, the standalone container requires an existing PostgreSQL database reachable from the container. Set the `ARTEX_PG_*` variables below. The example uses Docker Desktop's `host.docker.internal` to reach PostgreSQL on the host. On native Linux Docker Engine, add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to `docker run` for a host database, or use the reachable hostname of your database server. ```bash docker pull ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest mkdir -p data keys docker run -d --name artex \ --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \ -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 \ -p 127.0.0.1:8788:8788 \ -e ARTEX_PG_HOST=host.docker.internal \ -e ARTEX_PG_PORT=5432 \ -e ARTEX_PG_USER=artex \ -e ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD='yourpass' \ -e ARTEX_PG_DBNAME=artex \ -e ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE=disable \ -e ARTEX_JWT_KEY_DIR=/app/keys \ -v "$PWD/data:/app/data" \ -v "$PWD/keys:/app/keys" \ ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest # → http://localhost:8787 (docker logs artex | grep "Setup token") ``` In `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.ghcr.yml`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is passed to ARTEX as its own variable. The server percent-encodes it into the connection URL, so a password may contain `/`, `?`, `%`, `@`, `:` or spaces. In `.env`, quote a value that contains `#`, and write `$$` for a literal `$`. The `ARTEX_PG_*` variables take the password raw; quote it in a shell. The image includes a scanner toolchain (`nmap`, `nuclei`, `httpx`, `katana`, `ffuf`, `dalfox`, `sqlmap`, `ripgrep`, `curl`, `npm`, …) and built-in `/app/skills`. The GHCR Compose file below persists `./keys` and `./data`; it does not mount a host `skills/` directory, so the image's built-in skills are used. #### Compose stack from the prebuilt image `docker-compose.ghcr.yml` runs the same ARTEX + PostgreSQL stack from the released image, with no checkout build. The image is not published yet: v0.7.0 predates the GHCR publish step, so use the checkout build above until the next tagged release. Once the first image is published, download the file and `.env.example` once: ```bash curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/main/docker-compose.ghcr.yml curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/main/.env.example cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD, optionally an LLM key docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml pull docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up -d # → http://localhost:8787 (docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml logs artex | grep "Setup token") ``` Update the stack without a git checkout: ```bash docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml pull docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up -d ``` Pin a version with `ARTEX_IMAGE_TAG=v0.7.1` in `.env` (or `0.7.1`); unset uses `latest`. To use custom skills, copy them into a host directory and add `- ./skills:/app/skills` to the `artex` volumes, which overrides the built-in `/app/skills`. For remote MCP you can choose `http` (Streamable HTTP) or `sse` (legacy SSE) in system settings. Legacy SSE servers usually establish the event stream with `GET /sse` and receive JSON-RPC over `/message?sessionId=...`; configure the URL as `/sse` and send `Authorization: Bearer `. ### Option 3: prebuilt binaries (Releases) Download the zip for your platform from [Releases](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases). It contains `artex`, `start.sh` (`start.bat` on Windows), `skills/` and `config.example.json`: ```bash cp config.example.json config.json # fill in the database connection ./start.sh # → http://localhost:8787 ``` Start with `start.sh` / `start.bat`, not `./artex`: it is a daemon script that restarts the process after a backoff. To keep it in the background: `nohup ./start.sh >artex.log 2>&1 &`. #### Verifying a release Each release attaches `SHA256SUMS` and a CycloneDX SBOM, `artex-.cdx.json` (Go modules in the linux/amd64 binary, the frontend `package-lock.json`, `go.mod`/`go.sum`), next to the zips. The zips also carry a GitHub build provenance attestation. Releases published before this was added have neither. ```bash sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS # add --ignore-missing if you downloaded only some zips gh attestation verify --repo BaaRai/ARTEX # built by this repository's release workflow ``` ### Option 4: build the single binary from source ```bash cd web && npm ci && npm run build:static && cd .. cp -r web/out server/webui/dist CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags embedui -o artex ./cmd/artex ./start.sh ``` Only `-tags embedui` embeds the frontend into the binary. ### Option 5: cross-platform release archives `build.sh` builds and embeds the frontend, strips debug info, and writes zips for Linux amd64/arm64, macOS amd64/arm64 and Windows amd64 by default: ```bash ./build.sh --release # output: dist/artex--*.zip ARTEX_TARGETS=linux/amd64,windows/amd64 ./build.sh --release ./build.sh --target linux/amd64 --upx ``` UPX is disabled by default: self-extracting binaries may be incompatible with some kernels, virtualization environments or security policies. Pass `--upx` only after confirming the target runtime supports it. --- ## Configuration **Database** (`config.json`, `ARTEX_PG_DSN`, or `ARTEX_PG_*` environment variables — see [External PostgreSQL](#external-postgresql)): ```json { "database": { "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 5432, "user": "artex", "password": "yourpass", "dbname": "artex", "sslmode": "disable" } } ``` **LLM**: `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-...` (or `OPENAI_API_KEY`), or configure it in the UI's "LLM Configuration" page, which can also add a local Ollama server as a keyless provider (format "Ollama", default base URL `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`). Optional: `ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER` (`anthropic | openai | openai-responses | ollama | bedrock-gateway`), `ARTEX_LLM_MODEL`, `ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL`, `ARTEX_LLM_PROXY`. **Base URL gotcha**: for the Anthropic format, enter the host **without** `/v1` (for example `https://api.anthropic.com`); ARTEX appends `/v1/messages`. OpenAI-format providers append `/chat/completions` (or `/responses` for `openai-responses`), so their base **does** end in `/v1` (for example `https://api.openai.com/v1`). **OpenAI-compatible gateways**: any provider that serves an OpenAI-style `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint works through the **OpenAI** format — no dedicated format needed. Create a profile with format **OpenAI**, set **Base URL** to the gateway's `/v1` root, paste the key, then click the **↻** button next to *Model* to load the provider's catalog (`GET /v1/models`) and pick a model; models the provider adds later appear on the next refresh. For example, [NotHoly](https://notholy.com) (offensive-security models) uses base URL `https://api.notholy.com/v1` with an API key from its console. **Bedrock gateway**: select **Bedrock gateway** in System → LLM for a gateway that exposes the Bedrock `InvokeModel` and `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` paths and accepts bearer-token authentication. Enter the gateway's base URL (for example, `https://gateway.example.com/bedrock`), the full Bedrock model ID, and the token in **Bearer token**. If required, enter static headers as one `Name: Value` per line in **Custom gateway headers**. ARTEX adds `/model/{model}/invoke` (or `/invoke-with-response-stream`), sends `anthropic_version: bedrock-2023-05-31`, and decodes Bedrock's binary event stream. Enter the model ID manually; this gateway format does not have a model-list operation. The token and custom header values are encrypted in the database and are write-only in the UI. Editing the gateway URL requires re-entering the token, so saved credentials cannot be sent to a different host by changing the URL. This format is for bearer-authenticated gateways; direct AWS Bedrock with SigV4 credentials is not supported. For environment-based setup, set `ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER=bedrock-gateway`, `ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL`, `ARTEX_LLM_MODEL`, and `ARTEX_LLM_API_KEY`. Optional `ARTEX_LLM_CUSTOM_HEADERS` uses the same newline-separated `Name: Value` format. **Task archive storage**: local disk by default. Set `ARTEX_ARCHIVE_STORAGE=s3` to store cold task packages in an S3-compatible bucket and release their local package space after verification. Existing local archives remain usable. See [Task archive storage](docs/task-archive-storage.md) for configuration, permissions, integrity checks, temporary disk requirements and recovery. **Concurrency**: work agents per task, in "System Settings" (default 3). **Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results for the worker, planner, chat and main agent are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Unset or empty, the boundary is on; set `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0` (or `false` / `off` / `no`) to disable it. Cost: about 154 bytes per tool result plus one system note. **Noise profile (off by default)**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE` paces the requests ARTEX sends to targets (WebFetch, HTTP custom tools, the enrich probe). Unset or `off` keeps today's behaviour: no limit, no cache. `quiet` = 2 req/s per host (burst 4, 1 in flight), `balanced` = 5 req/s (burst 10, 2 in flight), `aggressive` = 20 req/s (burst 40, 4 in flight). A profile adds jitter, backs off on 429/503 (honours `Retry-After`, bounded retries, GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only), deduplicates identical in-flight GETs and caches them briefly (60/30/10 s; never POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), and logs a per-host noise line each minute. `ARTEX_TARGET_USER_AGENT` sets a User-Agent on target requests that carry none. With traffic capture on, Bash commands that use the proxy (curl, wget, python-requests) are paced too, per host by the same rate and jitter, and counted in the same per-host lines. The in-flight caps, retries and cache apply only to ARTEX's own requests. This is best effort, not a security boundary. Raw scanners such as nmap are not paced, and neither is a command that bypasses the proxy (`--noproxy`, a removed proxy variable). With capture off, nothing launched from Bash is paced. The low-and-slow prompt block supplies the rate flags in every case. The **Target noise** card in System settings sets the profile at runtime (no restart) and shows the per-host counters; once saved, that setting takes precedence over `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE`. **Scanner User-Agent (opt-in per task)** adds a stable ARTEX User-Agent to supported target requests so defenders can correlate them with an approved assessment. See the [configuration and WAF triage guide](docs/scanner-user-agent.md). **Low-and-slow agent guidance (off by default)**: when a noise profile is set, the planner, worker, main agent and chat agents receive a code-owned prompt block with the profile's per-host limits and exact rate/delay flags for the installed scanners. It tells them to test one host at a time, back off on 429/503 and never raise the rate to meet a deadline. **Run budgets (off by default)**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a task's total spend (planner rounds and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Unset or `0` means unlimited. A worker is not started when the remaining task budget cannot cover its estimated cost (the average of finished workers, else 50,000 tokens and 10 turns). Near the wrap-up reserve (the larger of 5% and 20,000 tokens, and 2 turns) the task enters a forced wrap-up: the planner writes a summary and final goal judgment, and workers may only write back. The task then ends `done` if its goals are met, else `timeout`. Practical floor: below 50,000 tokens no worker starts; 50,000-70,000 typically gives one worker then wrap-up; pick well above 70,000 for real exploration. Planner, worker, judge, and compactor rows in `llm_usage` are counted back into the cap when a ledger is created, including after a restart and after a revived run drops its ledger. A restored task already inside the wrap-up reserve does not get another worker: only that reserve remains, and the run wraps up. Chat, goal decomposition, and side questions are stored on the same task and are not counted. The per-worker average is not restored (usage rows have no run boundary), so the estimate starts from the defaults until a worker finishes in this process. **Common flags**: `./start.sh -addr :8787 -proxy :8788` (`-addr` frontend/API, `-proxy` traffic recording proxy). ### External PostgreSQL ARTEX already supports an external PostgreSQL 16+ instance — the `postgres` service in `docker-compose.yml` is only the bundled default. Because the database is startup configuration and the system's single source of truth, there is no runtime database switcher in the UI: change the environment variables and restart the server to point at another instance. Configure the connection with either a full connection string or individual parts: - **`ARTEX_PG_DSN`**: full PostgreSQL connection URL (for example `postgres://artex:pass@db.example.internal:5432/artex?sslmode=require`). When set, it takes precedence over the `ARTEX_PG_*` variables and you are responsible for percent-encoding any URL-special characters in the username or password. - **`ARTEX_PG_*` parts** (recommended when passwords contain `/`, `?`, `%`, `@`, `:`, or spaces — ARTEX percent-encodes the user and password and removes `ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD` from the environment at startup): - `ARTEX_PG_HOST` — PostgreSQL host - `ARTEX_PG_PORT` — PostgreSQL port (default `5432`) - `ARTEX_PG_USER` — database user - `ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD` — database password (raw, not URL-encoded) - `ARTEX_PG_DBNAME` — database name - `ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE` — TLS mode (`disable`, `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`) #### Compose without the bundled `postgres` service To run ARTEX against an external PostgreSQL server with Docker Compose, remove the `postgres` service, the `depends_on` block, and the `pgdata` volume from `docker-compose.yml`, and point `artex` at your database: ```yaml services: artex: image: ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest security_opt: - "no-new-privileges:true" environment: # Option A: individual parts (recommended; percent-encodes special characters) ARTEX_PG_HOST: ${ARTEX_PG_HOST:?Set ARTEX_PG_HOST in .env} ARTEX_PG_PORT: ${ARTEX_PG_PORT:-5432} ARTEX_PG_USER: ${ARTEX_PG_USER:-artex} ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD: ${ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD:?Set ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD in .env} ARTEX_PG_DBNAME: ${ARTEX_PG_DBNAME:-artex} ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE: ${ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE:-require} # Option B: full DSN (overrides ARTEX_PG_* when set) # ARTEX_PG_DSN: ${ARTEX_PG_DSN} ARTEX_JWT_KEY_DIR: /app/keys ports: - "${ARTEX_BIND_ADDR:-127.0.0.1}:8787:8787" - "127.0.0.1:8788:8788" volumes: - ./data:/app/data - ./keys:/app/keys restart: unless-stopped ``` #### Local disk usage (`data/`) Moving PostgreSQL to an external host does **not** move the runtime `data/` directory off local disk. `data/` still stores spilled HTTP/TCP traffic blobs (`data/traffic/_blobs`), LLM transcripts, task working files, and local task archives, so heavy workloads can still fill the host disk if `data/` is on a small volume. Mount `data/` on a suitably sized volume, and consider setting `ARTEX_ARCHIVE_STORAGE=s3` (see [Task archive storage](docs/task-archive-storage.md)) to offload cold task archives to object storage. ### Reverse proxy deployment (HTTPS / exposing only 443) The frontend, API and SSE stream share port 8787 (the binary listens on `127.0.0.1:8787` by default; the Docker container publishes on `127.0.0.1`), and the activity stream is same-origin by default, so **no `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` is needed**: expose 443 and keep 8787 internal. SSE keeps a long-lived connection with continuous pushes, so the proxy **must disable buffering**; otherwise the browser connects but never receives events. Redirect plain HTTP first, so a bookmarked `http://` URL never reaches the app unencrypted: ```nginx server { listen 80; server_name your.domain.com; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } ``` Then the TLS server: ```nginx server { listen 443 ssl; server_name your.domain.com; # ssl_certificate / ssl_certificate_key ... location / { # 512 MiB combined file limit plus 1 MiB of multipart metadata. client_max_body_size 513m; proxy_request_buffering off; proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; # SSE essentials: buffering off, long timeouts, HTTP/1.1 proxy_buffering off; proxy_cache off; proxy_read_timeout 3600s; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection ""; } } ``` **Login rate limit behind a proxy**: login allows 10 attempts per minute per client IP. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address, so without further setup all users share one budget and an attacker who fails 10 logins blocks everyone, admin included, for up to 15 minutes. Keep the `X-Forwarded-For` line and set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (comma-separated CIDRs, empty by default) to the address ARTEX sees the proxy connect from: - **nginx and ARTEX both on the host** (binary, `./start.sh`): the peer is `127.0.0.1`; start ARTEX with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1/32`. - **nginx on the host, ARTEX in Docker** (`docker-compose.yml`): the connection reaches the container from the Docker bridge gateway (a `172.x` address), not from `127.0.0.1`. Find it with `docker network inspect artex_default --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}'` (the network is `_default`), put `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=/32` in `.env`, then `docker compose up -d`. For a peer in that list, ARTEX reads `X-Forwarded-For` from the right and takes the first address that is not a trusted proxy; from any other peer the header is ignored. Trust only proxies you run: a trusted peer can claim any client address. **Security headers**: every response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a same-origin referrer policy and a `frame-ancestors 'self'` CSP; console documents additionally get a `Permissions-Policy` and COOP/CORP. `Strict-Transport-Security` is sent only when the request is known to be HTTPS: directly over TLS, or via `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` from a trusted proxy. The same list above enables it, so with nginx in front, the 443 server answers with HSTS after you set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES`. > Only when SSE needs a different origin from the page (e.g. a dedicated subdomain) should you set > `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` **at build time** (it is baked into the static bundle during `next build`; > setting it at container runtime has no effect). --- ## Operations ### Troubleshooting an empty tool call In the task's session transcript, expand the affected tool call and compare **Command** and **Output**. The `UNTRUSTED_OUTPUT` markers identify the boundary around tool output. They are expected and should stay enabled while troubleshooting. - **Command shows `{}`.** The recorded tool input is an empty JSON object. For a tool that requires a command, this means its command argument was missing. Check which model and version produced the call. - **Command shows `(empty)` or `(failed to load)`.** The transcript has no input detail to display or could not fetch it. If the session record contains a command, include that discrepancy in a report. - **Output shows `[]`.** This is the recorded result body. Check the row's success or failure indicator and its input separately before drawing conclusions about what ran. For a recurring problem, share the ARTEX version or commit, the model and version, and a sanitized excerpt of the affected input and result. Remove credentials, target data, and other sensitive content before sharing. ### Backups `scripts/backup.sh` dumps the Postgres database (and optionally the data directory) with timestamped output and rotation: ```bash scripts/backup.sh --with-data # db dump + data/ archive, keep 14 scripts/backup.sh --keep 7 # db only, keep 7 ``` Restore into a running stack: ```bash gunzip -c backups/artex-db-.sql.gz | docker compose exec -T postgres \ psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" ``` Stored secrets (LLM API keys, proxies and gateway custom headers, MCP env, task credentials, notification channel config, Brave/Tavily search keys, web search and global proxies, the execution spec of custom tools, the capture-proxy rewrite rules) are encrypted in the database with the key in `keys/secret.key` (generated at first start, mode 0600, next to `jwt.key`). **A database backup without that key cannot restore those secrets**: back up `keys/` with the dump, separately. Deployments without a persistent disk set `ARTEX_SECRET_KEY` (32 bytes, base64 or hex, e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`). ARTEX refuses to start when the database holds encrypted secrets and no key is available. Daily cron example (03:20, operator crontab): ``` 20 3 * * * cd /path/to/ARTEX && scripts/backup.sh --with-data >> backups/backup.log 2>&1 ``` ### Updating and upgrading > Upgrading swaps the program and never touches data: the Postgres volume `pgdata`, `./data` > (traffic index, task files, transcripts), `./keys` (`jwt.key`, `secret.key`) and `./skills` are > preserved. **No manual database step is needed**: on every start ARTEX applies its embedded > `schema.sql` baseline, then any pending numbered migration from `db/migrations/`, in order, each > in its own transaction. Restarting the new binary is the upgrade. Back up `./data`, `keys/` and > the database before upgrading. **Update banner (opt-in, off by default)**: start ARTEX with `ARTEX_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to ask the public GitHub releases API for the latest tag, at most once per 24 hours (cached in memory; a failed check is not retried within that window). When the release is newer, the web UI shows a dismissible strip linking to Releases. The request sends only `User-Agent: artex-update-check`. Unset, ARTEX makes no update request and shows no banner. #### Upgrading from a clone made before 2026-10-23 The repository history was rewritten that day to drop a personal email address from the commit metadata. A clone made before then cannot fast-forward, and `./update.sh` now stops instead of silently rebuilding stale code. Recover once, then upgrade normally: ```bash git stash # only if you have local changes git fetch origin git reset --hard origin/main git stash pop # only if you stashed ``` Your data is unaffected: `./data`, the `pgdata` volume and `./skills` are not part of git history. #### Option 1: one-click update script ```bash cd ARTEX ./update.sh ``` The script optionally `git pull`s, then offers **① Docker update** (`docker compose build artex` → `docker compose up -d artex`) or **② local build update** (rebuild the frontend static assets, then recompile `./artex`; restart the process for it to take effect). #### Option 2: Docker (Compose or GHCR image) ```bash cd ARTEX git pull docker compose build artex docker compose up -d artex docker image prune -f # optional ``` If running the prebuilt `ghcr.io/baarai/artex` container directly, pull the new tag (`docker pull ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest` or a pinned `:v`) and recreate the container with the same `/app/data` and `/app/keys` mounts. If you run the prebuilt Compose stack, the update is: ```bash docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml pull docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up -d ``` #### Option 3: prebuilt binaries Download the new zip, stop the old process, overwrite `artex` and `skills/` (keep `config.json` and `data/`), then restart: ```bash cp -r /skills ./ && cp /artex ./ ./start.sh ``` #### Option 4: build from source ```bash git pull cd web && npm ci && npm run build:static && cd .. cp -r web/out server/webui/dist CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags embedui -o artex ./cmd/artex # restart ./start.sh ``` --- ## Development ```bash ./dev.sh # backend(:8787) + traffic proxy(:8788) + frontend next dev(:5173) → http://localhost:5173 ``` - Backend: `go run ./cmd/artex` (without `-tags embedui`, the frontend is not embedded) - Frontend: `cd web && npm run dev` (`/api` is reverse-proxied to the backend, with hot reload) - Tests: `go test ./...` - Reproduce the fast CI checks locally: `./scripts/verify.sh` (add `--full` for `-race` and the static web build; add `--security` for `govulncheck`) - Security scan: install `govulncheck` and run `./scripts/verify.sh --security` (CI runs this on every push and pull request) - Mock preview (no backend): `cd web && NEXT_PUBLIC_MOCK=1 npm run dev` --- ## Architecture ARTEX is an **LLM multi-agent-driven autonomous penetration testing system**: a Go monolithic backend (with the Next.js UI embedded) + PostgreSQL. Agent capabilities come from the [`norma`](https://github.com/Autumn-27/norma) SDK (`agentcore` / `tool` / `permission` / `harness` / `memory` / `transcript`). At its core is the **dual-graph architecture**, plus two autonomy mechanisms: **process-level information exchange between workers** and the **planner's multi-round shared todolist**. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph FE["Frontend Next.js (go:embed embedded single binary)"] UI["Dashboard · Tasks · Assets · Coverage graph · Traffic · Workspace · System settings"] end subgraph SRV["server (Go net/http)"] API["REST /api/* JWT auth SSE"] ENG["engine scheduling loop"] MGR["Manager task/engine/store lifecycle"] end subgraph AG["agent (norma SDK)"] GO["goals goal decomposition + scope extraction"] PL["planner the planner (sole intent generator)"] WK["worker executor ×N"] MA["mainagent human-in-the-loop"] end subgraph DB["PostgreSQL"] AGRAPH["Asset graph assets / companies / task_scope"] EGRAPH["Exploration graph exploration_nodes / anchors / activity"] end subgraph SUB["Supporting subsystems"] PROXY["Traffic recording proxy MITM + CA tracing"] GUARD["guard / intercept tool approval gate"] ENR["enrich DNS / HTTP async enrichment"] EXT["MCP · skills · memory · report"] end UI -->|HTTP| API API --> MGR --> ENG ENG --> PL ENG --> WK API --> MA API --> GO PL --> DB WK --> DB MA --> DB GO --> DB WK -->|"Bash / HTTP fully traced"| PROXY WK --> GUARD WK --> ENR PL -.-> EXT WK -.-> EXT MA -.-> EXT ``` | Layer | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | **Frontend** | Next.js static export embedded via `go:embed`; tasks, assets, exploration and coverage graphs, traffic, human-in-the-loop chat | | **server** | `net/http` routing, JWT auth, SSE; `Manager` owns tasks, engines and DB stores | | **engine** | One `plannerLoop` + N worker goroutines per task; intent claiming, timeout/pause/drain | | **agent** | goals / planner / worker / mainagent; `ToolSet` exposes the dual graphs as LLM tools | | **db** | PostgreSQL persistence (pgx); embedded schema and numbered migrations applied at startup | | **Supporting** | Recording MITM proxy, approval gate, async enrichment, MCP/skills/memory/report | For the code-level map (execution flow, trust boundaries, decisions) see [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md); for startup, configuration precedence, backup and key rotation see [docs/OPS.md](docs/OPS.md). --- ## Security Please report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub Security Advisories; see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Operational security properties: - **Secrets at rest**: LLM keys/proxies/gateway headers, MCP environment, task credentials, notification config, search keys, proxies, custom-tool execution specs, capture-proxy rewrite rules and traffic evidence snapshots are encrypted with AES-256-GCM using `keys/secret.key` (or `ARTEX_SECRET_KEY`). ARTEX refuses to start when encrypted data exists and no usable key is available. - **First-run claim**: `/setup` requires a one-time token printed at startup; the UI binds to `127.0.0.1` by default. - **Login protection**: 10 attempts per minute per client IP, with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` for correct client attribution behind a reverse proxy. - **Untrusted tool output**: framed as data for every agent by default (prompt-injection boundary). - **Release integrity**: SHA-256 sums, CycloneDX SBOM and GitHub build provenance attestations for release archives. --- ## About this project This repository is the actively maintained community continuation of ARTEX, originally by [Autumn-27](https://github.com/Autumn-27). It diverges from the original with its own features and fixes, tracked in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md), under the same AGPL-3.0 license. The original repository is no longer public, so the link points to the author profile. --- ## References and prior art - [Cairn](https://github.com/oritera/Cairn) - Approval-details UI inspired by [AegisHook](https://github.com/RuoJi6/AegisHook) --- ## License and disclaimer ### Open source license This project is licensed under the **GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL-3.0)**; see the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for the full terms.
